source: ACOG - Elevated Blood Pressure in Pregnancy & Up to 6 Weeks Postpartum (urgent care protocol, hosted by Urgent Care Association)
verification: numbers checked against ACOG-derived protocol + UT Southwestern; 'same day' and home-recheck wording is my translation, needs clinician review
content: A postpartum blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher (top number 140 to 159, or bottom number 90 to 109) is abnormal and can mean postpartum preeclampsia, even if there are no symptoms. High blood pressure can appear for the first time after delivery, so it should not be ignored just because she feels fine. Have her rest quietly for a few minutes and recheck. If it is still 140/90 or higher, she should contact her provider the same day. If she also has a severe headache, blurred vision, or pain in the upper right belly or upper stomach, treat it as an emergency. The ACOG protocol covers pregnancy and up to six weeks after delivery.

source: ACOG - Elevated Blood Pressure in Pregnancy & Up to 6 Weeks Postpartum (urgent care protocol, hosted by Urgent Care Association)
section: Elevated Blood Pressure With Severe Symptoms
verification: checked against ACOG-derived protocol
example_phrases: my head is killing me and my BP is up
blurry vision and high blood pressure
pain in the top of my stomach
content: A blood pressure of 140 to 159 systolic or 90 to 109 diastolic together with any of these is treated as preeclampsia with severe features and needs immediate emergency care: a severe headache, blurred vision, or pain in the upper right abdomen or upper middle stomach. She should call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room now and tell them she recently gave birth.

source: ACOG - Elevated Blood Pressure in Pregnancy & Up to 6 Weeks Postpartum (urgent care protocol); University of Iowa severe hypertension protocol
verification: numbers checked against two protocols; home-recheck wording needs clinician review
content: A blood pressure of 160 systolic or higher, or 110 diastolic or higher, is a severe-range reading and counts as preeclampsia with severe features even with no other symptoms. Severe hypertension is confirmed when it lasts 15 minutes or more, and hospital treatment is meant to start within 30 to 60 minutes to lower the risk of stroke. She should recheck while arranging care, not wait for symptoms, and call 911 or go to the emergency room if it stays in this range or if she has any warning symptoms. Tell them she recently gave birth.

source: Kansas Perinatal Quality Collaborative - Acute Hypertension in Pregnancy & Postpartum Algorithm (ACOG-based); UT Southwestern
verification: secondary (state quality collaborative); numbers consistent across sources
content: A blood pressure below 140 systolic and below 90 diastolic is not in the elevated postpartum range (about 120/80 is a typical healthy reading). Reassure her and encourage continued checks, but do not use a normal reading to dismiss warning symptoms such as a headache that will not go away, vision changes, or upper belly pain. Symptoms still matter even when the number looks fine.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs
section: Headache That Will Not Go Away
verification: CDC page text checked. NOTE: CDC lists a persistent or worsening headache as a warning sign by itself, not only with vision changes
content: CDC lists a headache that will not go away or gets worse over time as an urgent maternal warning sign for the year after delivery. It is more concerning if it feels like the worst headache of her life, or if she has high blood pressure or swelling elsewhere. She should contact her provider right away, and if she cannot reach them, go to the emergency room or call 911. If it comes with vision changes, a high blood pressure reading, or upper belly pain, treat it as an emergency (RED). Remind her to say she recently gave birth.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs; Kansas Dept. of Health and Environment Hear Her flyer
section: Preeclampsia-Related Warning Signs (Vision, Swelling, Belly Pain, Vomiting)
verification: CDC list checked; combination rule (headache + vision) follows CDC/ACOG logic, needs clinician review
example_phrases: pain in my stomach that won't go away
throwing up and it's not normal
content: CDC's urgent warning signs include changes in vision, extreme swelling of the hands or face, severe belly pain that does not go away, and severe nausea and vomiting that is not like morning sickness. Any of these can point to postpartum preeclampsia. A headache together with vision changes, or any of these together with high blood pressure, needs emergency care now: call 911 or go to the ER and say she recently gave birth. A single sign on its own still calls for contacting her provider right away.

source: Standard emergency guidance (no direct source verified; ACOG protocol references eclampsia)
verification: conservative emergency rule; add a primary citation (ACOG or CDC) before the final submission
example_phrases: she is shaking and not responding
content: A seizure, uncontrollable shaking, or loss of consciousness after giving birth is a life-threatening emergency and can be linked to eclampsia, a complication of high blood pressure. Call 911 immediately. If someone is with her, they should call for her.

source: CDC Hear Her (warning sign); Baylor Scott & White Health; Ascension patient library
verification: CDC lists heavy bleeding as a warning sign; pad-an-hour and golf-ball numbers confirmed in two health-system sources (not CDC). Earlier draft said 'egg-sized' - sources say golf ball
example_phrases: I'm soaking a pad every hour
I feel dizzy and I'm bleeding
content: Heavy vaginal bleeding after pregnancy is an urgent warning sign. Seek emergency care if she soaks through a pad in an hour or less, passes clots larger than a golf ball, has bright red bleeding that suddenly gushes after it had slowed, or feels dizzy, faint, weak, or has a racing heartbeat with the bleeding. Call 911 or go to the ER and say she recently gave birth.

source: Baylor Scott & White Health - Postpartum bleeding: what's normal and what's not
verification: secondary (health system blog); stage timing and 6-week range vary slightly across sources
example_phrases: I'm still bleeding after two weeks
content: Bleeding after birth (lochia) is normal and usually lasts several weeks, up to about six weeks and sometimes a little longer. It starts bright red with small clots in the first days, then lightens to pink or brown, and may start and stop. Small clots are expected early on. Reassure her unless she has any of the heavy-bleeding signs (soaking a pad an hour, clots bigger than a golf ball, sudden bright red gushing) or a foul smell or fever, in which case use the emergency or provider guidance instead.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs
section: Trouble Breathing, Chest Pain, Fast Heartbeat
verification: CDC page text checked
example_phrases: I need to prop up with pillows to breathe
content: Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast-beating heart are urgent maternal warning signs. Trouble breathing includes struggling to breathe when lying flat (needing to prop up with pillows to sleep) or being unable to catch her breath so that talking and breathing are both difficult. These can signal a blood clot in the lungs or a heart problem. Call 911 or go to the ER now and say she recently gave birth. Do not wait to see if it improves.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs; Ascension patient library
section: Leg Swelling, Redness, or Pain (Possible Blood Clot)
verification: CDC page text checked; escalation to RED when combined with chest or breathing symptoms follows CDC logic, needs clinician review
example_phrases: my calf hurts and is red
my leg is warm and sore
content: Swelling, redness, or pain in a leg (or arm) is an urgent maternal warning sign and can mean a blood clot. She should get medical care right away, and if she cannot reach her provider, go to the emergency room. If it is combined with chest pain, trouble breathing, or a racing heartbeat, call 911 immediately.

source: CDC Hear Her - Warning Signs poster; Ascension patient library
verification: threshold confirmed on CDC Hear Her poster and a health-system discharge sheet
content: A temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher after delivery is an urgent warning sign and may mean an infection such as a uterine, wound, urinary, or breast infection. She should contact her provider right away, and go to the emergency room if she cannot reach them or feels very unwell. Remind her to say she recently gave birth.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs
verification: CDC list checked; escalation rule follows bleeding/chest guidance, needs clinician review
content: Dizziness or fainting is an urgent maternal warning sign. She should contact her provider right away or go to the ER if she cannot reach them. If she faints, or has dizziness with heavy bleeding, chest pain, or trouble breathing, call 911.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs
verification: CDC page text checked
example_phrases: I have no energy at all
I can't get through the day
so tired I can't get out of bed
content: CDC lists overwhelming tiredness, meaning she does not have enough energy to get through her day, as an urgent warning sign. It is different from the ordinary tiredness of caring for a newborn. Ask what she can and cannot manage, and encourage contacting her provider, since it can come with anemia, infection, heart problems, or depression.

source: Texas DSHS Hear Her Texas (CDC campaign materials)
verification: secondary, partial text only; confirm wording on the full document
content: It is normal to feel tired and have some pain after giving birth, especially in the first weeks. Offer reassurance, rest tips, and encourage help from family. Escalate only if tiredness is overwhelming, pain is severe or getting worse, or any warning sign appears (fever, heavy bleeding, bad headache, vision changes, chest pain, trouble breathing, leg swelling).

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms
section: Trust Your Instincts and Say You Recently Gave Birth
verification: CDC page text checked
content: The warning-sign list does not cover every symptom. If something does not feel right or she is unsure whether it is serious, she should talk to her provider, and she should always say she is pregnant or was pregnant within the last year. If she cannot reach her provider, she should go to the ER or call 911. Take her concern seriously even if it is not on a list.

source: Providence health system; Ascension patient library (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (health systems); recovery duration varies
example_phrases: my incision hurts a little but it's getting better
I feel numb near the scar
content: Soreness around a C-section incision, some numbness, and cramping called afterpains (often stronger while breastfeeding) are normal, along with vaginal bleeding that lasts a few weeks. The incision can take up to about six weeks to heal. Keep it clean and dry, support it with a pillow when coughing or standing, and avoid lifting anything heavier than the baby. If pain is steadily improving and there is no fever, redness, or discharge, offer reassurance.

source: Ascension patient library; University of New Mexico Health patient education (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (health systems); fever threshold varies by clinic (100 to 101 F), 100.4 F used to match CDC
example_phrases: my incision is red and hot
content: After a C-section, call the provider if the incision has redness that is getting worse or feels hot, pain or drainage that is increasing, a foul smell, or if the incision opens, or if she has a fever of 100.4 F or higher or chills. Mild, steadily improving soreness is expected; worsening is the signal.

source: Ascension patient library - After a Cesarean (paraphrased)
section: Other Reasons to Call the Provider
verification: secondary (health system patient education); clinician review needed
example_phrases: I haven't pooped in a week
content: She should contact her provider if she has burning with urination or blood in her urine, vaginal discharge with a foul odor, no bowel movement within a week after birth, a rash or hives, or a sore, red, painful area on a breast (possibly with flu-like symptoms, which can mean mastitis). These are common and treatable but should be checked. Fever or severe belly pain with any of these should be treated as urgent.

content: Mild nipple soreness in the first week or two and breast fullness when milk comes in are common. Check the latch, feed often, and use comfort measures. No fever and no hard, red, hot area means no urgent action is needed.

source: CDC - Symptoms of Depression Among Women (paraphrased); JAMA PRAMS 2018 summary
verification: primary page text checked
example_phrases: why do I feel so bad after having my baby
content: About 1 in 8 women with a recent live birth report symptoms of postpartum depression, and rates vary by state from about 1 in 10 to nearly 1 in 4. It is common and treatable, and most people get better with treatment. Use this to reassure her that she is not alone and that nothing she did caused it.

source: CDC - Symptoms of Depression Among Women (paraphrased)
verification: primary page text checked
example_phrases: I feel nothing for my baby
I don't think I'm a good mom
content: Symptoms of postpartum depression can include crying more often than usual, feeling angry, feeling distant from the baby, and doubting her ability to care for the baby. A lasting sad, anxious, or empty mood is also a core sign. If these last more than two weeks, are severe, or interfere with daily life, encourage her to contact her healthcare provider soon and offer to help find support.

source: CDC; California Dept. of Public Health; clinical sources (paraphrased)
verification: secondary sources; duration varies from days to about 2 weeks
example_phrases: I feel overwhelmed but it's only been a few days
content: The baby blues are common, with tearfulness, mood swings, irritability, and feeling overwhelmed that start in the first days after birth and usually ease on their own within days to about two weeks. Reassure her, encourage rest and help, and check in again. If symptoms last longer than two weeks, are severe, or get worse, treat it as possible postpartum depression. Postpartum depression is not limited to the first two weeks.

source: Derived from CDC and clinical sources (product rule, not a quoted guideline)
section: Low Mood Lasting More Than a Week (Watch)
verification: DERIVED RULE - clinician must confirm the Watch cutoffs; the risk engine, not retrieval, should set Watch
example_phrases: I've been down for a week
content: If low mood, tearfulness, or anxiety has lasted most of a week or is not easing, check in again within a few days, ask about sleep, appetite, and support, and offer a repeat mood screen. Move to AMBER if it passes two weeks, interferes with daily life, or the screen score rises.

source: California Dept. of Public Health; Minnesota Dept. of Health (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (state health departments)
example_phrases: it's been months and I still feel awful
my baby is 6 months old and I'm not okay
content: Postpartum depression and anxiety can start during pregnancy or at any point in the baby's first year and can last for months. Risk is higher with a personal history of depression or anxiety, lack of social support, intimate partner violence, young maternal age, or loss of an infant, but it can happen to anyone. Ask how long symptoms have lasted and encourage contacting a provider if they persist or affect daily life.

source: EPDS validation literature (Scientific Reports, 2023 meta-analysis); scale copyright Royal College of Psychiatrists
verification: literature checked; cutoffs of 10 and 13 both widely used; ask the clinical advisor which one the app uses. Do not put the EPDS questions in the app without permission
content: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale has 10 items scored 0 to 3 (total 0 to 30). Cutoffs of 10 or higher (possible depression) and 13 or higher (probable depression) are both widely used, with validation studies spanning roughly 9 to 13. Suggested routing: 10 to 12 means encourage a provider conversation soon; 13 or higher means contact a provider promptly. A screening score is not a diagnosis. Item 10 is handled separately regardless of the total.

source: EPDS validation literature (Scientific Reports, 2023 meta-analysis)
verification: literature checked; clinician review needed for the response wording
example_phrases: I answered yes to the self-harm question
I sometimes think about hurting myself
content: Any answer above zero on EPDS item 10 (thoughts of self-harm) needs a same-day safety follow-up, whatever the total score. Do not assume intent: research found many positive answers reflect fleeting thoughts of escaping problems with no plan, and some people misread the question. Ask calmly and directly whether she is having thoughts of ending her life or hurting herself. If yes, or if unsure, give 988 (call or text) and, if she is in immediate danger, 911.

source: CDC Hear Her (warning sign); HRSA National Maternal Mental Health Hotline; 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
verification: CDC lists thoughts of hurting yourself or your baby as a warning sign; hotline scope confirmed via HRSA announcement; clinician review needed for response wording
example_phrases: everyone would be better off without me
content: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, or a plan or intent to act, are an emergency. Respond with care, stay with her in the conversation, and direct her to call or text 988 right away, or call 911 if she is in immediate danger. Encourage her to tell a partner or family member now. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-852-6262) is not an emergency line, so in a crisis use 988 first.

source: MGH Center for Women's Mental Health; CDC Hear Her (warning sign); Texas DSHS Hear Her toolkit (paraphrased)
section: Intrusive Thoughts About the Baby (Distressing, Unwanted)
verification: secondary (academic medical center). NOTE: CDC lists thoughts of harming yourself or your baby as a warning sign, so do not dismiss. Clinician review needed
example_phrases: I keep picturing something bad happening to my baby
scary thoughts about dropping the baby
I'm afraid I'll hurt my baby but I don't want to
content: Unwanted, upsetting thoughts or images about harm coming to the baby are common after birth, and many mothers with postpartum depression or anxiety have them. When she is frightened or disgusted by the thoughts, does not want to act on them, and knows they are not real wishes, they are not evidence that she is dangerous. Reassure her and tell her she is not alone, but also encourage her to tell a provider or perinatal mental health specialist soon, since CDC lists these thoughts as a sign to get care and they can be treated. Do not treat as an emergency unless a RED condition applies.

source: Penn State Health; WBUR clinical interview (paraphrased)
section: Thoughts About Harming the Baby: When It Is an Emergency
verification: secondary; clinician review required before shipping
example_phrases: I think the baby would be better off if I ...
voices are telling me to hurt the baby
content: Thoughts of harming the baby become an emergency when she wants to act on them, feels no distress or aversion about them, has a plan, or also has confusion, hallucinations, paranoia, or delusions. This pattern is different from distressing intrusive thoughts. Call 911 or go to the nearest ER, make sure someone stays with her and the baby, and do not leave her alone with the baby while she waits for help.

source: MGH Center for Women's Mental Health; Penn State Health; HHS Office on Women's Health (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (academic medical center, federal fact sheet); clinician review needed
example_phrases: I haven't slept in days and feel amazing
someone is trying to take my baby
content: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. Signs include hallucinations, delusions or paranoia (for example believing someone wants to harm her or the baby), severe confusion, extreme agitation, racing or manic energy, and very little need for sleep. It usually begins within the first two weeks after birth and occasionally later. A family history of bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis raises risk. Direct her to call 911 or go to the ER now, and urge a partner or family member to stay with her.

source: HHS Office on Women's Health - Perinatal Mental Health Conditions fact sheet (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (federal fact sheet; partially read); confirm details
example_phrases: my heart is racing and I can't relax
I keep checking the baby over and over
content: Postpartum anxiety can show up as constant worry, racing or intrusive thoughts, trouble sleeping even when the baby sleeps, dizziness, or hot flashes. Postpartum OCD involves upsetting repeated thoughts (obsessions) and actions repeated to calm them (compulsions), and the mother usually knows the thoughts are disturbing. These are common and treatable. Encourage contacting a healthcare provider and offer Postpartum Support International (call or text HELP to 1-800-944-4773).

source: CDC; Rhode Island Dept. of Health (paraphrased)
verification: general claim checked on CDC page; medication and breastfeeding details need clinician review
example_phrases: will I be on meds forever
can I take medicine while breastfeeding
content: Depression after birth is treatable, and most people get better with treatment. Options commonly include talk therapy, medication, or both, chosen with a provider based on severity and personal preference. Many mothers can continue breastfeeding while treated, but the choice of medication should be made with a provider, who can check lactation safety resources such as NIH LactMed. The assistant should not recommend or change any medication.

source: HRSA National Maternal Mental Health Hotline; Postpartum Support International; 988 Lifeline
verification: numbers confirmed across multiple sources; reconfirm before the demo
example_phrases: I need help but don't know where to start
content: The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline is free, confidential, and open 24/7 by call or text at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), in English and Spanish, with interpreter services in many languages. It offers counseling support and referrals for pregnant and postpartum people and their loved ones, but it is not an emergency line. Postpartum Support International's helpline is 1-800-944-4773 (call or text HELP) for information, support groups, and provider referrals. For suicidal crisis, call or text 988; for immediate danger, call 911.

source: California Dept. of Public Health; Minnesota Dept. of Health (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (state health departments)
example_phrases: I don't want anyone to think I'm failing
content: Reassure her that postpartum depression and anxiety are not her fault and not a sign of weakness or bad parenting, and that asking for help is a healthy step that benefits both her and her baby. Practical supports to suggest: asking friends or family for childcare so she can rest, protecting sleep where possible, and telling her provider how she has been feeling. Do not wait for a screening appointment if symptoms are present now.
